query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor, uniformly dispersed amount (1–2 wt%) of coated nano-ZrO2 particles in the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will significantly enhance its mechanical integrity (e.g., increasing compressive strength by 30–50% relative to the unmodified alloy) while maintaining its large caloric response under applied magnetic and pressure fields.
generation.material_initial_state: The baseline (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy exhibits a robust caloric response but suffers from poor integrity and crack susceptibility under operating conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1–2 wt% of surface-coated nano-ZrO2 particles in-situ during melting, followed by rapid solidification under an inert atmosphere to ensure uniform dispersion.
generation.conditions: Process the alloy during melting with controlled addition of coated nano-ZrO2 under an inert atmosphere. Follow with rapid solidification to lock in the particle dispersion. Mechanical and caloric tests will be performed under similar applied magnetic and pressure field conditions, as well as temperature and cyclic loading regimes used in prior studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform dispersion of surface-coated nano-ZrO2 particles both within the alloy matrix and along the grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The coated nanoparticles act as reinforcement agents that impede crack initiation and propagation through dispersion strengthening and crack deflection mechanisms. Their coating minimizes adverse interfacial reactions, ensuring that the nanoparticle inclusion does not interfere with the martensitic or structural phase transformations responsible for the large caloric response.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength by approximately 30–50% over the baseline (surpassing approximately 218 MPa) is expected, while the alloy retains its large caloric response under the same operational field conditions.
generation.baseline: The unmodified (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy exhibits high caloric performance but has limited compressive strength due to cracking and poor structural integrity.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under operational conditions similar to prior studies (applied magnetic and pressure fields, operating temperatures, and loading regimes) and within the composition and processing space that maintains a rare-earth–free system.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the complete inertness of the coated particle interfaces during thermal cycling, and slight modifications in the phase transformation kinetics may occur if nanoparticle dispersion is not optimal.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one batch of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy with the optimized in-situ dispersion of coated nano-ZrO2 particles and one control batch without nanoparticles. Subject both batches to identical processing conditions, followed by mechanical testing (e.g., compressive strength and fracture toughness tests) and caloric response measurements (under applied magnetic and pressure fields) across the relevant temperature range.
measurements: Caloric response magnitude (e.g., entropy/temperature changes under field cycling)
Microstructural analysis (particle dispersion uniformity, grain boundary integrity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticle-enhanced samples do not show a statistically significant increase (≈30–50%) in compressive strength compared to controls, or if they exhibit a diminished caloric response or unfavorable phase transformation behavior, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: NiAl-based composites reinforced by CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) particles were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure, mechanical, and tribological properties of the NiAl-HEA composites were investigated. Microstructural analyses show that after SPS, the HEA phase homogenously distributed in the NiAl matrix. Non-uniform diffusion of various elements occurred during the high temperature sintering process. Transmission electron microscope (TEM) observation of the composites revealed that many nano particle of Al2O3 generated at the grain boundary. The yield strength significantly increased after adding HEA particles. The compressive strength of the composites increased with the contents of HEA increasing, which should be attributed to the second phase hardening effect of HEA particles and fine grain strengthening effect. The composite of 10 wt.% HEA exhibited significant room temperature compressive properties, with the ultimate compressive strength of 2692 MPa and the compressive strain of 34.2%, respectively. The results of the wear tests show that the addition of HEA will reduce the wear resistance of composites to some

Second phase hardening effect of HEA results in the difficulty of dislocations movement. Particle clustering produces high local stress concentration, thus it provides more crack nucleation sites and lower energy propagation routes. All compressive strains of composites are equal to or lower than that of 0 wt.% HEA. The similar results were also reported by Refs [,]. Brittle interfacial reaction products are commonly generated in metal matrix composites []. According to the STEM images, as shown in Figure 6 and Figure 7, many nano particles located in the grain boundary. When compared with 0 wt.% HEA, the numbers of nano particles at the grain boundary is significantly increased after the addition of HEA and the grain size is decreased, which lead to the increase of yield strength. Figure 8 shows the fracture surfaces of 0 wt.% HEA and 15 wt.% HEA composites, respectively. The fracture mode of 0 wt.% HEA is intergranular fracture (Figure 8b). The HEA phase of 15 wt.% HEA composite showed a river-like pattern, which indicates the plasticity of HEA phase decreases after high temperature reaction diffusion.

proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor in‐situ dispersion of rare‐earth–free oxide nanoparticles (e.g., 1–2 wt% nano-ZrO2) during melting.
proposals.conditions: Melt the alloy with a controlled addition of nano-ZrO2 under inert atmosphere, followed by rapid solidification to lock the dispersion. Caloric response measured under applied magnetic and pressure fields at operating temperatures similar to prior studies.
proposals.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed nano-ZrO2 particles within the matrix and at grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: The nanoparticles impede crack initiation and propagation (dispersion strengthening and crack deflection mechanism) without significantly disturbing the phase transformation dynamics responsible for the caloric effect.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The composite alloy should exhibit increased compressive strengths possibly by 30–50% relative to the baseline (sufficiently surpassing 218 MPa) while retaining a large caloric response under applied fields.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single intervention enhances structural integrity via nanoparticle toughening while leaving the bulk caloric phase essentially unchanged, thus achieving rare-earth-free improved strength and high caloric performance.

proposals.intervention: Minor doping with a ductile element such as Cu (around 2–3 at.%) to promote grain refinement.
proposals.conditions: Introduce Cu during alloy synthesis followed by controlled solidification and appropriate thermal cycling to achieve fine equiaxed grains; test under the same applied-field and pressure-field conditions used in baseline caloric measurements.
proposals.structural_mediator: A refined, homogeneous grain structure with strengthened grain boundaries.
proposals.mechanism: The addition of Cu facilitates dynamic recrystallization resulting in grain refinement, which improves toughness and suppresses crack propagation without interfering with the martensitic/structural transition driving the caloric effect.
proposals.predicted_outcome: An expected enhancement in mechanical integrity (increased compressive strength, ideally comparable or above the 218 MPa mark) with little to no detriment observed in the caloric response magnitude.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By refining the grain structure through a simple compositional tweak, the alloy becomes mechanically robust while preserving the phase characteristics essential for high caloric performance.

proposals.intervention: Apply a targeted laser surface remelting treatment to create a hardened, fine-grained surface layer.
proposals.conditions: Utilize a high-energy laser to remelt only the outer ~50–100 µm of as-cast samples, followed by rapid solidification; subsequent caloric and mechanical tests under cyclic applied magnetic and pressure fields at target operating temperatures.
proposals.structural_mediator: A refined, compressively stressed surface layer over the unaltered bulk.
proposals.mechanism: The laser remelting induces controlled solid-state phase transformation and rapid re-solidification, forming a fine-grained, high-strength surface that combats crack initiation and propagation, while the bulk remains unaffected, maintaining its intrinsic caloric transformation behavior.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Overall improvement in integrity (fewer and smaller surface microcracks and increased effective compressive strength) combined with preserved caloric response from the unmodified core.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This surface-focused intervention decouples the mechanical failure sites from the caloric active bulk, ensuring robust integrity without sacrificing the caloric performance, all within a rare-earth–free scheme.

proposals.intervention: Implement severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion, HPT) as a post-processing step to homogenize and refine the microstructure.
proposals.conditions: Subject the alloy to HPT at room temperature under pressures of ~6–8 GPa for several rotations (e.g., 5–10 turns) followed by annealing at moderate temperatures to relieve excessive strain while retaining grain size refinement. Test under applied-field and pressure-field loading regimes.
proposals.structural_mediator: A uniformly refined ultrafine-grained structure with reduced residual stress concentrations.
proposals.mechanism: Severe plastic deformation refines the microstructure and promotes a homogeneous distribution of defects, significantly enhancing toughness and resistance to cracking while preserving the short-range order needed for the caloric effect.
proposals.predicted_outcome: A measured increase in fracture toughness and compressive strength (targeting improvements similar in range to or exceeding alternative approaches) while maintaining the original large caloric response due to the unchanged fundamental phase transformation characteristics.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single-step processing intervention offers a structural route to overcome cracking issues through microstructural refinement without altering the transformation mechanism underpinning the caloric response, thus fulfilling the rare-earth-free criterion.

critiques.addresses_problem: The approach directly targets the poor integrity and cracking by introducing oxide nanoparticles that can hinder crack initiation and propagation.
critiques.constraints: It keeps the alloy rare‐earth–free by selecting an inert oxide (nano-ZrO2) and does not require altering the bulk composition significantly.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of dispersion strengthening and crack deflection is physically sound; uniformly dispersed nanoparticles can impede crack propagation without interfering heavily with the transformational events that drive the caloric response if well distributed.
critiques.feasibility: In‐situ nanoparticle dispersion via controlled melt processing and rapid solidification is feasible with established metallurgical techniques, though interfacial reactions must be carefully managed.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from HEA composites shows that nanoparticle additions can increase yield strength via second phase hardening (e.g., PMC6212883), though there is also a cautionary note on particle clustering generating stress concentrations.
critiques.main_risk: Risk lies in nanoparticle agglomeration or the formation of brittle interfacial phases that might inadvertently alter the phase transformation responsible for the caloric effect.
critiques.fix: Introduce surface treatment or coating on the nanoparticles to improve interfacial compatibility and ensure uniform dispersion during processing.

critiques.addresses_problem: Severe plastic deformation via HPT aims to refine the microstructure and eliminate stress concentrators, thereby reducing cracking.
critiques.constraints: The process is rare‐earth–free and performed post-fabrication, which means the alloy composition remains intact; however, the impact on the caloric transformation must be carefully considered.
critiques.physical_soundness: Grain refinement and homogenization are well-known to improve mechanical properties, yet the drastic microstructural changes might modify the transformation behavior underpinning the caloric response.
critiques.feasibility: HPT and subsequent moderate annealing are established methods in processing HEAs, as supported by literature in similar alloy systems.
critiques.evidence: Previous studies in CoCrNi HEAs processed by HPT demonstrate significant improvements in strength and ductility (see PMC7512411 records), though care must be taken to avoid altering the intrinsic transformation curves.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the severe plastic deformation may shift or dampen the caloric effect if the refined microstructure alters the martensitic or structural transformation behavior.
critiques.fix: Optimize a subsequent annealing step to relieve excessive strain and recover the original caloric transformation characteristics.

critiques.addresses_problem: Minor Cu doping is intended to promote grain refinement and improve toughness, thereby reducing cracking without a major overhaul of the alloy system.
critiques.constraints: This intervention remains within the rare‐earth–free requirement and preserves the overall alloy composition with only a small adjustment.
critiques.physical_soundness: Doping with a ductile element like Cu is known to facilitate dynamic recrystallization, leading to a refined grain structure; however, its impact on the phase transformation driving the caloric response needs careful assessment.
critiques.feasibility: Incorporating a few atomic percent of Cu during alloy synthesis is feasible using conventional melting and casting techniques with controlled thermal treatment.
critiques.evidence: Similar approaches in alloy systems have shown that small additions can refine grain structure and boost mechanical integrity (as discussed in studies on grain boundary engineering in HEAs, e.g., PMC7264233), though direct evidence for Cu in this system is less explicit.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that even minor Cu doping might alter the transformation temperatures or kinetics, leading to a potential sacrifice in the caloric response.
critiques.fix: Conduct a systematic phase diagram and transformation behavior study for small Cu additions to ensure that the caloric response is not diminished.

critiques.addresses_problem: Laser surface remelting creates a hardened, fine-grained surface layer that can hinder crack initiation while leaving the bulk—where caloric transformation occurs—almost unaffected.
critiques.constraints: This method is rare‐earth–free and designed to be a surface treatment, thus preserving the bulk caloric properties under applied-field and pressure-field conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound if the laser treatment is carefully controlled to only affect the surface layer, ensuring that the caloric active bulk stays intact; however, thermal gradients and phase mismatches at the interface are concerns.
critiques.feasibility: Laser surface remelting is an established technique in materials processing and can be finely tuned for depth and energy input.
critiques.evidence: Studies on laser surface heat treatment in HEA systems (e.g., PMC11012396 records) demonstrate that gradient or inverse gradient structures can yield significant improvements in mechanical integrity while maintaining favorable bulk properties.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is the possibility of creating detrimental stress gradients or inducing unwanted phase changes at the surface-to-bulk interface that could eventually compromise the overall performance under cyclic loading.
critiques.fix: Precisely control the laser remelting parameters to confine the treatment to a thin, controlled surface layer and verify that the bulk caloric properties remain unaffected.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly targets the cracking issue by introducing oxide nanoparticles for dispersion strengthening. Although there is a risk of nanoparticle agglomeration or deleterious phase formation that could affect the caloric phase transformation, this can be mitigated by applying a surface coating to the nano-ZrO2 particles. Compared to the other options, this approach minimally perturbs the bulk alloy composition and transformation mechanisms, thereby preserving the large caloric response while enhancing mechanical integrity. Supporting evidence from PMC6212883 shows that nanoparticle additions increase yield strength via second phase hardening, and the proposed coating fix directly addresses the main risk.
